title: Decomposing Out-of-Distribution Error in Conditional Flow Matching via Wasserstein Geometry
claim: A regularized model keeps out-of-distribution error bounded and smooth, while the baseline's error is dominated by geometric distortion and oscillates beyond the training range.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; line plot then paired stacked-area plots with dashed ID/OOD boundary
description: The figure has two parts. Panel (a) is a line plot of Wasserstein distance against condition strength c. A black dotted curve shows the intrinsic ground-truth drift. A green line shows the robust model's error and a red line shows the baseline's error. A vertical line at c=4 separates the in-distribution region from a shaded OOD region. All three curves stay near zero before c=4. After c=4 the red baseline oscillates sharply up to about 20, while the green robust model rises smoothly to about 12 and stays above the dotted drift curve. Panel (b) has two side-by-side stacked-area plots, titled 'Baseline Model: High Geometric Distortion' and 'Robust Model: Controlled Distortion'. Each splits the error into grey interpolation sparsity and a colored geometric distortion area, red for the baseline and green for the robust model. The eye goes first to the jagged red area. Bold captions sit below each panel.
caption: Exact validation on linear drift manifold. These results confirm that spectral regularization converts the high-variance failure
abstract: Conditional flow matching has emerged as a powerful generative modeling framework that learns a vector field to transport an initial distribution toward a target data distribution. However, theoretical understanding of its out-of-distribution (OOD) performance under unseen conditions remains limited. In this work, we establish a rigorous geometric formulation to decompose the source of generalization error. We treat the conditional task as a map from the condition space to the Wasserstein space and derive a generalization bound under a coarse embedding assumption. The resulting decomposition separates OOD error into three tractable components: Interpolation Sparsity , Geometric Distortion , and In-Distribution Fit . Our empirical evaluation confirms that this framework demonstrates three key functions: (1) it acts as a diagnostic tool that tracks the dynamics of generalization during training; (2) it identifies dataset-specific failure modes (e.g., topological gaps, geometric instability); and (3) it enables mathematically motivated interventions that yield predictable gains by minimizing specific terms.
